entries.title: Learning can open a path to freedom
entries.quote: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
entries.attribution: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VI
entries.summary: Douglass describes realizing that literacy was connected to the power slavery tried to deny him. Knowledge did not erase the injustice around him, but it gave him a clearer understanding of how that system worked and strengthened his determination to learn. The passage treats education as more than information: it can make dependence visible and create room for purposeful action.
entries.question: What knowledge would make you less dependent on someone else’s interpretation of your choices?

sources.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VI

entries.title: Understand the strongest objection
entries.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
entries.attribution: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter II
entries.summary: Mill argues that a belief is poorly understood if we have never seriously engaged with the strongest reasons against it. Explaining an opposing view fairly can reveal whether a disagreement is about evidence, priorities, or the meaning of the claim—not just expose a weak version that is easy to dismiss.
entries.question: Which belief of yours could you defend against the strongest opposing argument, rather than the easiest one to dismiss?
